beginner: Bok choy likes loose, rich soil with plenty of compost that holds moisture but still drains well. Steady, even moisture keeps the leaf-stalks crisp and mild and keeps the plant from bolting; dry, hard soil stresses it and pushes it to flower.
seasoned: Bok choy grows best in a fertile, well-drained yet moisture-retentive loam or sandy loam high in organic matter, held at even moisture (UMN). As a fast, shallow-rooted leafy brassica it responds to compost worked in before sowing, which feeds quick growth and buffers the steady moisture that keeps the leaf-stalks crisp and tender. Uneven moisture both stresses the plant toward bolting and contributes to tipburn of the inner leaves, and keeping the soil out of the strongly acidic range also helps hold down clubroot, the brassica-family soil disease.

beginner: Bok choy grows best in soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, about 6.0 to 7.0. A simple soil test tells you where you stand. Keeping the soil from getting too acidic also helps prevent clubroot, a cabbage-family soil disease.
seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0. Bok choy is forgiving and grows well across roughly 5.5 to 7.5: UMN and NCSU both give 6.0 to 7.5 for Chinese cabbage and bok choy, while Clemson lists 5.8 to 6.5. As with other brassicas, holding the soil toward neutral rather than strongly acidic also helps suppress clubroot, so a grower with clubroot history should lean to the high end.

beginner: Bok choy grows fast and likes steady nitrogen for tender leaves and stalks. Mix some compost or a balanced fertilizer into the soil before planting, then give it one light feeding a couple of weeks after the seedlings come up. Because the crop is so quick, you usually do not need to feed it much more.
seasoned: Bok choy is a fast leafy brassica that runs on nitrogen for quick, tender growth, but the crop is so quick that one or two light feedings are plenty. Work compost or a balanced fertilizer into the bed before sowing, then side-dress lightly with nitrogen about 2 to 3 weeks after emergence to push crisp, mild leaf-stalks. Clemson gives the cole-crop rate of 5-10-10 worked in before planting, then about 34-0-0 side-dressed; for a 30-to-50-day crop, keep it light, since lush late growth draws aphids and does little for a plant you will cut soon.

beginner: Time to give your bok choy a light feeding.
seasoned: Time to side-dress your bok choy with a little nitrogen.

beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 at planting, then one light nitrogen feed a couple of weeks after the seedlings come up.
seasoned: High N for fast, tender leafy growth: a balanced 5-10-10 or 10-10-10 worked in before planting, then a light nitrogen side-dress such as 21-0-0, calcium nitrate, or blood meal 2 to 3 weeks after emergence. Do not overfeed a quick crop.

beginner: Follow the label rate for a balanced vegetable fertilizer at planting, then one light nitrogen feed beside the plants a couple of weeks later.
seasoned: Work in 5-10-10 at about 3 pounds per 100 square feet before planting (Clemson), then side-dress about a quarter cup of 21-0-0 (or 1 pound per 100 feet of row) once a few weeks after emergence; a compost-rich bed of baby bok choy often needs no extra feed.

beginner: Bok choy is small, fast, and easygoing, so it tucks in between slower crops. It grows well next to lettuce and other quick greens, bush beans, and aromatic herbs like dill, and alliums such as onions. The main thing is to keep it away from other cabbage-family plants, which share its pests and diseases, and to watch for flea beetles, which love it.
seasoned: Most bok choy companion pairings rest on space, timing, and tradition rather than measured effects. The practical ones are structural: bok choy is quick and shallow-rooted, so it interplants with lettuce and other fast greens and tucks beside legumes and aromatic herbs. Aromatic herbs and alliums are the traditional scent-based deterrents for the cabbage-family pests bok choy shares. The well-grounded caution is to separate bok choy from other brassicas, which share clubroot and the whole cole-crop pest complex, a rotation and disease principle more than a tested adjacency effect; bok choy is also a flea-beetle magnet, sometimes deliberately used as a trap crop near choicer brassicas.

beginner: Beans add a little nitrogen to the soil that the leafy bok choy can use, and the two share a cool-to-mild season without crowding each other.
seasoned: A legume interplant on nitrogen and structure: beans fix a little nitrogen the leafy bok choy draws on, and the quick bok choy uses the open ground between young bean plants. Sound space and timing logic rather than a measured bok choy effect.

beginner: Lettuce grows fast and low like bok choy, so you can sow them together to fill a salad bed, and both like the same cool weather.
seasoned: Bok choy and lettuce share a cool season, a shallow root zone, and a bed, so they interplant efficiently and are harvested young together. A space-and-timing pairing, not a documented growth boost; the two share no major pest.

beginner: Strong-smelling herbs like dill are a classic neighbor for cabbage-family plants; their scent is said to confuse pests, and their flowers bring in helpful insects.
seasoned: Aromatic umbels like dill are a traditional brassica companion, their flowers drawing the parasitoid wasps and hoverflies that attack brassica aphids and caterpillars. Let some flower nearby; treat it as a partial-mechanism aid rather than a measured bok-choy-specific effect.

beginner: Onions are a traditional neighbor for cabbage-family plants; their strong smell is thought to help put off the pests that hunt by scent.
seasoned: Alliums are a traditional brassica companion, their pungent scent thought to mask the crop from the cabbage-family pests that hunt partly by smell. Shallow-rooted and undemanding, they tuck around young bok choy without competing for much. A low-risk, scent-based aid rather than a proven control.

beginner: Keep bok choy away from other cabbage-family plants like cabbage, broccoli, kale, mustard, turnips, and radishes. They share the same pests and diseases, so grouping them makes flea beetles, caterpillars, and clubroot worse.
seasoned: Planting bok choy shoulder to shoulder with its brassica relatives, cabbage, broccoli, kale, mustard, turnip, radish, concentrates the family's shared pests (flea beetles above all, plus cabbage aphids, cabbageworms, loopers, diamondback moths, root maggots) and shared diseases in one spot, and repeated same-family planting lets soil-borne clubroot build up. Spread brassicas out and rotate where they grow each year.

beginner: Lots of tiny round shot holes peppering the leaves, made by tiny dark beetles that jump like fleas when you come near. Bok choy is one of their very favorite plants, and heavy damage can riddle or kill young seedlings.
seasoned: Small round shotholes pepper the foliage and the tiny dark beetles jump when disturbed. Bok choy and other mustards are highly preferred hosts, so pressure is often intense; seedlings can be stunted or killed and the holes mar the leaf-stalks of a crop eaten raw or lightly cooked.

beginner: Flea beetles are small jumping beetles that chew little pits and holes in cabbage-family leaves. They are drawn strongly to bok choy and mustards and hit small seedlings hardest, since a tiny plant cannot outgrow the damage.
seasoned: Crucifer flea beetles (Phyllotreta species) chew the foliage of brassicas and strongly prefer bok choy and mustard; adults overwinter in debris and emerge to attack the earliest, smallest plants, with multiple generations through the season.

beginner: Cover young plants with a light row cover from the day you sow, and if beetles are heavy use a spinosad spray. The main goal is to get the seedlings up and growing fast, before the beetles riddle them.
seasoned: Floating row cover from sowing is the most effective tool; spinosad helps under heavy pressure. The aim is rapid establishment past the vulnerable seedling stage, so push fast growth.

beginner: Use row cover from sowing, the single best defense, keep seedlings growing fast with steady water, and clear nearby cabbage-family weeds. Some growers plant a sacrificial mustard patch as a trap crop.
seasoned: Exclude beetles with row cover from sowing, keep seedlings vigorous with even water and a light feed, clean up crucifer weeds and crop debris, and consider an early trap planting of mustard to divert beetles from the main crop.

beginner: Clusters of small gray-green insects with a dusty, waxy coating on the new growth and tucked deep into the folds where the leaf-stalks meet, where they are very hard to wash out. Leaves may curl and there can be a sticky film.
seasoned: The gray-green, waxy-coated cabbage aphid forms dense colonies on growing tips and leaf undersides and lodges deep in the leaf-stalk folds, where it contaminates the harvested plant with insects and honeydew and is very hard to clean. Clemson notes aphid feeding yellows, stunts, curls, and wrinkles the foliage and brings sooty mold, with pressure heaviest on the fall crop.

beginner: Cabbage aphids are tiny insects that suck the plant's juices and breed fast. They love cabbage-family plants and hide down in the stalk crevices, which is the part you eat.
seasoned: Brevicoryne brassicae, a brassica-specialist aphid (with green peach aphid also present), sucks sap and reproduces rapidly; contamination of the harvested stalks with aphids and sticky honeydew is usually the real problem rather than plant stunting.

beginner: Knock colonies off with a strong spray of water and hit the undersides of leaves and the crevices with insecticidal soap or neem oil, repeating every few days. Welcome ladybugs and lacewings, which eat aphids.
seasoned: Dislodge colonies with a strong jet of water and spray insecticidal soap, neem, or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of leaf undersides and the stalk crevices; repeat every few days. Conserve natural enemies (parasitoid wasps, hoverflies, ladybugs).

beginner: Check the growing center and the stalk crevices often and act early. Go easy on nitrogen, since soft growth draws them, use row cover, and clear away old cabbage-family plants after harvest.
seasoned: Scout growing tips and the stalk crevices weekly and catch infestations before aphids lodge in the plant. Avoid excess nitrogen, use row cover on young plants, and destroy crop debris that carries them over.

beginner: Ragged chewed holes in the leaves, green caterpillars on the plants, and dark droppings. Because you eat the leaves and stalks, even a little chewing and mess is a problem.
seasoned: Ragged feeding holes with green or striped larvae and frass; the imported cabbageworm, cabbage looper, and diamondback moth larvae feed on bok choy (UMN lists all three), and on a fast leaf-and-stalk crop even light feeding and contamination downgrade the harvest.

beginner: Several white butterflies and moths lay eggs on cabbage-family leaves, and the caterpillars that hatch (imported cabbageworms, loopers, and small wriggling diamondback larvae) chew the foliage.
seasoned: The larvae of several brassica moths and butterflies feed on the foliage; the adults lay eggs on the leaves, and warm-region plantings see the most pressure. The diamondback moth is often the most numerous in the South.

beginner: Spray Bt, which is safe and targets only caterpillars, or pick them and their eggs off by hand from the undersides of leaves. Spray again after rain, since it washes off.
seasoned: Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki) or spinosad targeting young larvae and hand-pick where practical; repeat after rain, since Bt breaks down.

beginner: Use a row cover to keep the adults from laying eggs, clean up old cabbage-family plants and weeds, and check leaf undersides for eggs and small caterpillars.
seasoned: Exclude egg-laying adults with row cover, clean up brassica debris and weed hosts, and scout leaf undersides for eggs and early instars.

beginner: New transplants wilt and grow badly or fall over. If you pull one up, you'll find small white maggots eating the roots. It is worst in cool, wet spring soil.
seasoned: Transplants wilt, grow poorly, and may collapse; pulling a plant reveals small white maggots tunneling in the roots and lower stem. Damage is worst in cool, wet soil at spring establishment (UMN lists cabbage maggots among bok choy's pests).

beginner: A small fly lays eggs at the base of the plant, and the maggots that hatch burrow down and eat the roots. The fly is most active in cool, damp weather, so spring transplants are most at risk.
seasoned: The larvae of the cabbage root fly (Delia radicum) tunnel into brassica roots; the adult lays eggs at the stem base, and the maggots feed below, sometimes killing young plants and opening the door to rots.

beginner: Once the maggots are in the roots you can't save that plant, so pull and throw away the badly damaged ones. Put your effort into protecting the rest from new eggs.
seasoned: There is no effective rescue once maggots are in the roots; remove and destroy badly affected plants and protect the rest from further egg-laying.

beginner: Put a small collar or disk around the base of each transplant to stop the fly from laying eggs there, or use a row cover. Avoid planting into cold, soggy soil, and rotate away from where cabbage-family plants grew.
seasoned: Place a collar or disk around the stem base at transplanting to block egg-laying, or use row cover; avoid planting into cold, wet soil and rotate away from where brassicas grew.

beginner: Shield-shaped black-and-orange (or black-and-red) bugs on the leaves, which develop pale spots, then brown and look tattered. It is mostly a warm-region problem and loves cabbage-family plants.
seasoned: Shield-shaped bugs brightly marked black-and-orange or black-and-red feed with piercing-sucking mouthparts that leave pale stipples; affected leaves brown and look tattered, and heavy feeding wilts and deforms plants. A warm-region brassica specialist (Clemson).

beginner: The harlequin bug is a colorful stink-bug relative that pierces the leaves and sucks the juices, leaving pale blotches. It strongly prefers cabbage-family plants, especially in the South.
seasoned: The harlequin bug (Murgantia histrionica) specializes on cole crops, most damaging in the southern United States, where it completes several generations a year and overwinters as an adult in debris and weeds.

beginner: Search out and crush the bugs, their barrel-shaped eggs laid in rows, and the young ones by hand. Use a row cover to keep them off, pull badly infested plants, and clear away weeds and old plants where they hide over winter.
seasoned: Hand-pick and crush adults, nymphs, and the barrel-shaped egg rows; exclude with floating row cover; remove heavily infested plants. Insecticidal soap or neem helps where pressure is severe.

beginner: Clean up garden debris and cabbage-family weeds where the adults overwinter, use row cover, and consider a trap crop of mustard to lure them away from the main crop, then destroy it.
seasoned: Eliminate overwintering sites by removing crop debris and crucifer weeds, use row cover, and deploy an early trap crop of mustard to divert overwintering adults, then destroy it before the main crop is set out.

beginner: Ragged holes with smooth edges chewed in the low leaves and stalks, slimy trails on the plant and soil, and worst damage in cool, damp, shady spots and after rain.
seasoned: Smooth-edged holes in low foliage and tender stalks with silvery slime trails, worst in cool, wet, densely planted or heavily mulched beds; a succulent low green like bok choy is highly susceptible (NCSU lists slugs and snails).

beginner: Slugs and snails are soft, moisture-loving mollusks that feed at night and rasp holes in tender low greens like bok choy. They thrive in damp mulch and dense, shaded plantings.
seasoned: Several slug and snail species feed nocturnally, rasping the foliage; they shelter in moist debris and mulch by day and build up in cool, wet conditions.

beginner: Hand-pick at night or after rain, set out shallow traps, and use an iron-phosphate slug bait, which is pet-safe. Reduce damp hiding places and water in the morning so the surface dries by night.
seasoned: Hand-pick after dark or rain, use shallow traps and iron-phosphate baits (pet-safe), and remove daytime shelter; morning watering lets the surface dry before they feed.

beginner: Thin and space plants for airflow, keep mulch light near the plants, clear damp debris, and water early in the day rather than at dusk.
seasoned: Reduce moisture and shelter near the plants: thin for airflow, keep mulch off the crowns, clear debris, and irrigate in the morning rather than the evening.

beginner: Plants wilt in the afternoon, stay small and yellowish, and don't bounce back. If you dig one up, the roots are swollen into lumpy, club-shaped knobs.
seasoned: Plants wilt in the heat of the day, grow stunted and yellowed, and recover poorly; roots are swollen into distorted clubs and galls instead of normal fine roots.

beginner: A germ that lives in the soil infects the roots of cabbage-family plants and makes them swell, which stops the plant from taking up water and food. It stays in the soil for years.
seasoned: A soilborne organism (Plasmodiophora brassicae) infects brassica roots and forms the galls, which block water and nutrient uptake. It persists in soil for many years, spreads in contaminated soil and water, and infects most readily in acidic soils below about pH 6.5.

beginner: There's no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy infected plants. Keeping the soil from being too acidic (closer to neutral) helps hold it back, and growing cabbage-family plants only rarely in that spot starves the germ out.
seasoned: There is no cure once plants are infected; remove and destroy them. Raising soil pH toward neutral with lime suppresses the disease, and long rotations starve it out over time.

beginner: Don't grow bok choy or other cabbage-family plants in the same spot more than once every few years, longer if you've had clubroot. Keep the soil from being too acidic, improve drainage, and clean soil off your tools.
seasoned: Rotate brassicas out of affected ground on a long cycle (UMN advises up to 7 years where clubroot is known), keep soil pH up, improve drainage, and avoid moving infested soil on tools and boots.

beginner: Pale yellow blotches on top of the leaves, with fuzzy grayish growth on the underside, mostly in cool, damp weather. Bad cases discolor and spot the leaves and stalks.
seasoned: Pale yellow patches form on the upper leaf surface with a fuzzy gray-white growth underneath, mainly in cool, damp weather; severe infection discolors and spots the leaves and stalks. Bok choy's cool, humid season overlaps the weather it likes.

beginner: A mold-like disease that loves the cool, wet weather bok choy grows in, spreading through wet leaves and splashing water. Crowded plants and long leaf wetness make it worse.
seasoned: A fungus-like organism (Hyaloperonospora brassicae) that thrives in cool, wet, humid conditions and spreads by spores in water and air; long leaf wetness and crowded plantings favor it (Clemson).

beginner: Open up the airflow so leaves can dry, remove the worst leaves, and water at the soil instead of from above. It's hard to stop once the weather stays damp, so prevention matters most.
seasoned: Improve airflow and let foliage dry, remove badly affected leaves, and apply a copper-based fungicide if pressure is high; the disease is hard to stop once humidity stays high.

beginner: Space plants so air moves between them, water at the soil line, and pick resistant varieties if downy mildew is common where you live.
seasoned: Space plants for good air movement, water at the soil line rather than overhead, and choose resistant varieties where downy mildew is common.

beginner: Yellow patches shaped like the letter V appear at the leaf edges, pointing inward, with black veins inside them. It can spread through the plant and rot it.
seasoned: Yellow, V-shaped lesions spread inward from the leaf margins, with the veins inside the V turning black (Clemson); the disease moves through the vascular system and can rot the plant. Often the most serious brassica disease in warm, wet weather, and UMN lists it among bok choy's diseases.

beginner: A bacteria that often comes in on infected seeds or transplants. It gets into the leaves and travels through the plant's veins, spreading fastest in warm, wet weather.
seasoned: A seedborne bacterium (Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris) that enters through leaf pores and wounds and moves through the veins; it spreads in warm, wet conditions and on infected seed or transplants.

beginner: There's no real cure, so remove and destroy infected plants to keep it from spreading. Don't handle or brush against the plants while they're wet, because that spreads the bacteria.
seasoned: There is no effective cure; remove and destroy infected plants. Avoid working among plants when foliage is wet, since that moves the bacteria.

beginner: Begin with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants, don't plant where cabbage-family crops grew recently, space plants for airflow, and avoid overhead watering.
seasoned: Start with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants (a hot-water seed treatment helps), rotate 2 to 3 years away from brassicas, give plants room for airflow, and avoid overhead watering and handling wet foliage.

beginner: Small dark spots on the leaves that grow into round patches, often with rings like a tiny target. Bok choy is especially prone to it, and spotted leaves are not good to eat.
seasoned: Brown circular leaf spots with characteristic concentric rings (target spots) that enlarge and coalesce (Clemson); on a leaf crop even moderate spotting downgrades the harvest. Clemson notes Chinese cabbage and bok choy are more susceptible to Alternaria than common cabbage, and UMN lists it among bok choy's diseases.

beginner: A fungus that spreads in warm, wet weather and infects the leaves, leaving spots. It is worse on crowded, damp plantings and comes in on infected seed.
seasoned: Alternaria fungi (A. brassicicola, A. brassicae) infect brassica foliage, spreading by spores in wind and splashing water; infected seed, crop debris, and long leaf wetness drive them.

beginner: Remove and destroy spotted leaves and old plant debris, improve airflow so leaves dry quickly, and avoid wetting the leaves when you water. Start with clean seed.
seasoned: Remove spotted leaves and crop debris immediately, improve airflow, and avoid overhead watering; a copper-based fungicide can help under heavy pressure.

beginner: Use clean seed, rotate away from brassicas, space plants for airflow, water at the soil line, and clear crop debris after harvest.
seasoned: Use clean, disease-free seed, rotate away from brassicas, space for airflow, water at the soil line, and clear crop debris that harbors spores after harvest.

beginner: White, blister-like bumps on the undersides of the leaves, with yellow spots on top. Badly spotted leaves are not good to eat.
seasoned: White, blister-like pustules on leaf undersides with chlorotic spotting above; severe infection distorts and downgrades the foliage. A common brassica-greens disease, listed among bok choy's problems by NCSU and worse in mild, moist conditions.

beginner: A mold-like disease, not a true rust, that makes white pustules on cabbage-family leaves and spreads in cool, moist weather. It can ruin a leafy crop quickly.
seasoned: The oomycete Albugo candida, favored by cool nights, mild days, and leaf wetness; it spreads by splash- and wind-dispersed spores and survives on debris and as oospores.

beginner: Remove and destroy infected leaves, improve airflow, and water at the soil line. As with downy mildew, prevention works better than trying to cure it.
seasoned: Remove infected leaves and debris, improve airflow, and avoid overhead irrigation; chemical options are limited for the home garden.

beginner: Space plants out, avoid wetting the leaves, choose resistant varieties where it is common, and rotate your planting spot.
seasoned: Grow resistant cultivars where white rust is endemic, space for airflow, use drip irrigation, and rotate away from brassicas.

beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 inch a week.
seasoned: About 1 inch of water per week, kept as even as possible; bok choy is shallow-rooted and bolts faster and turns bitter under drought stress (UMN).

beginner: Aim for about 1 inch of water a week, a bit more when it is warm.
seasoned: Roughly 1 inch per week (UMN: about 1 inch of rainfall a week is good), more in warm, dry spells while the plants are sizing up.

beginner: Water at the base of the plants rather than over the leaves, which helps prevent leaf diseases.
seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose where possible to keep foliage dry and discourage leaf disease.

beginner: Lower leaves yellow and the plant looks soggy and limp, and seedlings may rot at the base.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves and limp growth; bok choy dislikes waterlogged soil, which invites damping-off in seedlings and crown and bacterial soft rot in cold, wet ground.

beginner: Wilting leaves that turn tougher and stronger-tasting, and a plant that bolts (flowers) sooner than it should.
seasoned: Wilting and stalled growth, then tougher, more pungent leaf-stalks and faster bolting; drought stress is a direct bolting trigger and also worsens tipburn of the inner leaves.

beginner: Keep the soil or tray damp while the seeds come up, without letting the surface dry out.
seasoned: Keep the seedbed or tray surface evenly moist through germination; brassica seed is shallow and should not dry mid-emergence.

beginner: Keep the young plants evenly damp as they grow. Bok choy has shallow roots, so keep the top of the soil damp.
seasoned: Grow the seedlings on with steady, even moisture. Bok choy is shallow-rooted, so keep the top few inches moist.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly damp through the few weeks of growth. If bok choy dries out, especially in warm weather, it bolts (flowers early) and turns bitter.
seasoned: Steady moisture through the few weeks of leaf-and-stalk growth matters most. Bok choy is shallow-rooted and bolts faster and turns bitter under drought stress, especially in a warm or lengthening-day spell, so never let it dry out.

beginner: Keep watering evenly and pick bok choy young, either the whole plant or outer stalks, before it bolts in warm weather.
seasoned: Keep even moisture and harvest the whole head or outer stalks young, before warm weather pushes it to bolt.

beginner: Keep the water steady so the stalks stay crisp and mild and the plant does not bolt early.
seasoned: Even, steady moisture is the whole game with bok choy: it keeps the plant growing fast, crisp, and mild and holds off the bolting that drought stress brings on.

beginner: Bok choy is best sown straight in the garden because it grows fast and does not like having its roots disturbed, though small transplants work too. Sow the seeds about a quarter to half an inch deep and thin to about 6 inches apart for baby plants or a foot for full-size ones. The big thing to avoid is a cold spell on young plants: more than about a week of nights below 50°F can make them flower (bolt) once it warms up. The fall crop is the most reliable. In hot areas, plant in fall through early spring instead of summer.
seasoned: Bok choy is fast and resents root disturbance, so it is often direct sown, though young transplants work well if set out before they become root-bound. Sow seed about 0.25 to 0.5 inch deep (NCSU) and thin to about 6 inches for baby types or 12 to 18 inches for full-size heads (NCSU; UMN). For transplants, start only about 3 weeks ahead and set out small. The timing trap is the cold-snap bolt: bok choy held more than about a week of nights below 50°F bolts once it warms, so avoid setting young spring plants into a long cold spell, and lean on the fall sowing, which is the more reliable crop. In hot regions, shift sowing to fall through early spring, since heat and long days force bolting.

beginner: A good-quality potting mix, not garden soil.
seasoned: A light, well-drained potting mix high in organic matter.

beginner: In mild areas, a pot of fall-sown bok choy can keep going through winter in a sheltered, sunny spot. In cold areas, move the pot against the house or into a cold frame, or cover it during hard freezes; bok choy takes light frost but a hard freeze damages it.

Watch for the cold-snap bolt: a pot of young plants chilled below 50°F for a week or more will run to seed when warmth returns.

A pot is also the easiest way to move the crop into shade or shelter as the weather turns or a cold snap threatens.

beginner: Other cabbage-family plants like cabbage, broccoli, kale, mustard, radishes, and turnips, because they share the same pests and diseases.
